<reason>Side A prevailed by establishing a decisive asymmetry between adjustable logistics and unadjustable adolescent circadian biology, effectively rebutting the bedtime compensation counterargument (which requires implausible full-hour nightly bedtime drift), and demonstrating that local alternatives cannot solve the collective action problem. While Side B raised legitimate economic concerns, Side A successfully framed these as manageable costs of change versus the developmental harms of the status quo, and clarified that the mandate protects the typical adolescent brain rather than imposing universal identical schedules.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 (A1) neutralizing the bedtime compensation challenge by arguing that erasing the sleep gain would require bedtimes to shift a full hour later every night, which conflicts with the biological constraint of delayed sleep onset in adolescents.</best_rebuttal>
